tasks.description: Ask the user for their name using input(), then print: Hello, {name}!
tasks.hint:
`input('prompt')` pauses execution and waits for the user to type something, then press Enter.
The result is always a string, stored in a variable: `name = input('Enter your name: ')`
Build the greeting with an f-string: `print(f'Hello, {name}!')`
tasks.walkthrough:
`input()` shows the prompt, waits for a line, and returns it as a string.
That string is saved as `name`, then dropped into the greeting with an f-string.

tasks.description: Ask the user for a number, then print that number multiplied by 2.
tasks.hint:
`input()` ALWAYS returns a string — even if the user types `5`, you get `'5'` (a string).
Convert it to a number before doing math: `num = int(input('Enter a number: '))`
Then multiply: `print(num * 2)`
tasks.walkthrough:
Whatever is typed comes back as text, so `int()` converts it to a whole number before it's stored.
After that, `number * 2` is ordinary maths.

tasks.description: Ask the user for two numbers on separate lines, then print their sum.
tasks.hint:
Use two separate `input()` calls, one for each number.
Convert both to `float()` so decimal inputs work: `a = float(input('First: '))`
Then `print(a + b)` — Python adds the numbers, not the strings.
tasks.solution:
a = float(input('First number: '))
b = float(input('Second number: '))
print(a + b)
tasks.walkthrough:
Two separate `input()` calls read two separate lines.
`float()` is used instead of `int()` so numbers like 2.5 work as well as whole numbers.
`a + b` adds the converted numbers rather than joining two strings.

tasks.description: Ask for a person's name and age. Print: My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.
tasks.hint:
Get both with separate `input()` calls and store in variables.
f-strings let you embed multiple variables: `f'My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.'`
Note: `age` is a string from input — you don't need to convert it if you're just printing it.
tasks.solution:
name = input('Name: ')
age = input('Age: ')
print(f'My name is {name} and I am {age} years old.')
tasks.walkthrough:
Both answers are read as strings, and that's fine here because they're only being printed, not used for maths.
The f-string has two placeholders and each is filled from its variable.

tasks.description: Ask the user to enter their favourite city. Print it in uppercase with 'I love ' in front.
tasks.hint:
Store the input in a variable: `city = input('Your favourite city: ')`
Call `.upper()` on it to convert to uppercase: `city.upper()`
Combine with string concatenation: `print('I love ' + city.upper())`
tasks.solution:
city = input('Your favourite city: ')
print('I love ' + city.upper())
tasks.walkthrough:
`city.upper()` makes an uppercase copy of the answer.
The `+` joins the fixed text and the uppercase city into one string. Note the space at the end of `'I love '`.

tasks.description: Ask the user for a number. Print 'Even' if it is divisible by 2, otherwise print 'Odd'.
tasks.hint:
Convert the input to `int` first: `num = int(input('Enter a number: '))`
The modulo operator `%` gives the remainder: `num % 2` is `0` for even, `1` for odd.
Use `if num % 2 == 0: print('Even') else: print('Odd')`
tasks.walkthrough:
`%` gives the remainder after division. Any even number divided by 2 leaves 0, any odd number leaves 1.
The `if` checks whether the remainder is 0 and prints the matching word.
You'll see a lot more of `if`/`else` tomorrow.

tasks.description: Ask the user for their first name and last name separately. Print their full name with a space in between.
tasks.hint:
Two `input()` calls: `first = input(...)` and `last = input(...)`
Join them: `print(first + ' ' + last)` or the f-string way: `print(f'{first} {last}')`
The f-string approach is cleaner — the space inside `{}` brackets is also part of the string.
tasks.solution:
first = input('First name: ')
last = input('Last name: ')
print(f'{first} {last}')
tasks.walkthrough:
Two inputs, two variables.
The space between the braces in the f-string becomes the space between the names in the output.
`print(first + ' ' + last)` would give exactly the same result.

lesson.intro:
So far your programs only talk. Today they listen. `input()` pauses the program
and waits for whoever is running it to type something. That one function is enough
to make programs that feel interactive.

In this app, when you run code that uses `input()`, a small box will ask you for
the answers first, one per line. Your program then reads them in order.

sections.heading: Asking a question
sections.body:
`input('...')` shows the text you give it, waits for a line of typing, and hands
that line back to you. You almost always store it in a variable.
sections.code:
name = input('What is your name? ')
print(f'Nice to meet you, {name}.')
sections.output: What is your name? Nice to meet you, Sam.

sections.heading: Whatever they type is text
sections.body:
This is the rule that catches everyone. `input()` always gives you a string,
even if the person typed `5`. You get `'5'`, and `'5' * 2` is `'55'`, not `10`.

If you want a number, convert it straight away with `int()` or `float()`.
sections.code:
answer = input('Pick a number: ')
number = int(answer)
print(number * 2)

sections.heading: Doing the conversion in one line
sections.body:
You can wrap `input()` inside `int()` directly. This is the most common way
you'll see it written. Use `float()` instead when decimals are allowed.
sections.code:
a = float(input('First number: '))
b = float(input('Second number: '))
print(a + b)

sections.heading: Joining text together
sections.body:
Two ways to combine strings. The `+` operator glues them end to end, and
you have to add spaces yourself. An f-string lets you write the sentence
naturally with the variables dropped in.

watch_out: Forgetting to convert. `input('Age: ') + 1` fails because you can't add 1 to text.
Using `int()` on something with a decimal point. `int('3.5')` is an error. Use `float()`.
Putting the conversion in the wrong place: `int(input('Enter a number: '))` converts the answer, which is what you want. `input(int('...'))` makes no sense.
In this app you have to supply the input values in the box before the program runs. If you supply fewer values than the program asks for, you'll see an EOFError.
